claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — one refuted (CL-0036), six still tracking, two new

Every open conditional claim (§4B — a specific, falsifiable test this system logs before the outcome is known, then grades against the data) is checked against Friday's close before any new narrative is written. Prices are Yahoo closes recorded in data/raw/claims_check_2026-10-10.json.

  • CL-0036 refuted — the claim said this week's rates-and-dollar jump was an orderly repricing that credit wouldn't treat as a risk event. Its refute line was a high-yield spread print of 3.15% or higher by 2026-10-15. The print dated 2026-10-08 (Thursday, the tech-selloff day), filled in this morning, came in at exactly 3.15%. That is two straight widenings since the claim was logged (3.03% → 3.09% → 3.15%), so the “credit doesn't care” read is refuted, plainly. For scale, 3.15% is mid-range on the high-yield spread's own roughly three-year record (64th percentile) — the claim tested direction, not an extreme, and the direction went against it.
  • CL-0039 still open, close to its refute line — Oracle's selloff as a durable repricing of AI-financing risk. Oracle rebounded to $141.40 Friday, +4.21% from the $135.69 base; a close of $142.47 (+5%) by 2026-10-16 refutes it. Tracking.
  • CL-0038 still open — Coherent's optics selloff as a genuine re-rating. Coherent closed at $312.62, +3.40% from the $302.35 base; +5% ($317.47) by 2026-10-16 refutes it. Tracking.

The claim's rate leg (the 10-year at or above 5.31%) failed again: Friday's 10-year was 5.24%. Confirmation is out of reach; only a refute or expiry is left. Due 2026-10-13.
  • CL-0032 still open — C.H. Robinson's RXO-deal selloff. CHRW closed at $142.31, +1.21% from the $140.61 base, well short of the +5% refute line. Due 2026-10-13.
  • CL-0035 still open — the storage re-test. Seagate closed at $783.00 (−2.81% from $805.63) and Western Digital at $397.28 (−3.35% from $411.04); neither has come near a +5% snapback. Due 2026-10-14.
  • CL-0037 still open — Caterpillar's downgrade selloff. CAT closed at $800.47, −1.64% from the $813.83 base. Due 2026-10-15.
  • CL-0040 opens — T-Mobile’s −13.27% on SpaceX’s spectrum deal (CNBC) is a durable repricing of the carriers’ competitive position, not a one-day overreaction. Test: T-Mobile’s return from Friday’s $148.58 close stays flat-to-lower over the next 5 trading days (confirms); a close of $156.01 (+5%) or higher through Friday 10-16’s close (graded on the 2026-10-19 run) refutes it.

dashboard_interp_html:
The short end led a small rise in yields on Friday. The 2-year rose 5bp to 4.80% (z +1.97) and the 3-month bill 2bp to 4.25% (z +2.31), while the 10-year rose 2bp to 5.24% (z +2.29) and the 30-year held at 5.60% (z +2.29). Every Treasury maturity is still flagged: higher than on all but a handful of days in the past six months. Short rates rising more than long rates flattened the curve (2s10s, the 10-year minus the 2-year, narrowed 3bp to 44bp). That's a bear flattener (Unit 1): the front end, which tracks expected Fed policy, did the moving. The 10-year first reached 5.24% on Sep 28 and has been there on 9 of the 10 sessions since; before this run, it last got there only briefly, in June 2007 (Monday's 5.31% peak was higher still; Today in history, below).

Thursday's real-yield data filled in, and it answers the question Thursday's drop left open. The 10-year fell 6bp that day. The 10-year real yield (what a bond pays after inflation, now dated 10-08) fell 5bp to 2.87%, and the 10-year breakeven (the bond market's inflation forecast) fell 1bp to 2.35%. So nearly all of Thursday's drop was real rates, not inflation expectations (Unit 2). On the TIPS record, which only starts in 2003, 2.87% is at or above the reading on 99.6 of every 100 days; this run peaked at 2.95% on Oct 5, a level last matched in Nov 2008, during the global financial crisis. The Cleveland Fed's longer model record puts real rates at the 80th percentile of the last 30 years but only the 54th since 1982.

Credit widened again on the selloff day, and that settles a claim. HY OAS (the extra yield investors demand to lend to junk-rated companies, dated 10-08) widened 6bp to 3.15% (z +3.53, the day's largest flag: higher than on all but one day in the past six months, the 3.24% of Oct 1). That is the print that refutes CL-0036 (Claims, above). It is not a record: HY OAS reached 4.61% in April 2025, and 3.15% sits at the 64th percentile of its own roughly three-year history. IG OAS (the investment-grade equivalent, dated 10-08) held at 0.82% (z +1.31, unflagged). So on Thursday's selloff, junk spreads widened while investment-grade spreads didn't move: a move confined to the riskiest borrowers so far (Unit 3).

The dollar (DXY, z +2.04) edged up 0.07% to 102.21: the 72nd percentile since 1971 (81st over 30 years), just under Wednesday's 102.24, a level last matched in April 2025. SOFR (the overnight bank funding rate, dated 10-08) eased 1bp to 3.87% (z +2.36). ON RRP (money funds' overnight parking spot at the Fed) was $0.30 billion (z −0.52, calm). The Fed's balance sheet and the Treasury's cash account (TGA) carry Wednesday's weekly readings until Thursday's next release.

Stocks rose broadly, but chips lagged again. The S&P 500 rose 0.59% to 7,811.54, 0.10% below its Oct 6 record close. The equal-weight proxy (RSP, the average stock) rose 0.55% against the cap-weight proxy (SPY) +0.60%, so the gain was broad, not just the biggest names. The chip fund SMH fell 0.65%: a fifth straight session behind SPY.

Why this matters: rising short-term yields keep money-market and CD rates high for savers, and the 10-year near 5.2% keeps mortgage rates elevated (7.40% this week). The new piece is credit: junk-bond spreads have now widened two prints in a row, while investment-grade hasn't moved. If a client holds a high-yield bond fund, that is the corner of the bond market where spreads widened on Thursday.
chart_of_day_why: Mechanical rule (§6.5a: largest |z| flag) points to HY OAS: z +3.53, ahead of SOFR's +2.36 (also dated 10-08) and the 3-month bill's +2.31. The print (dated 10-08, Thursday's selloff day) is the one that refutes CL-0036, which opened at 3.03% two sessions earlier (marked on the chart). The §4F context sits right next to the z-score: 3.15% is not a record (4.61% in April 2025) and sits at the 64th percentile of the high-yield spread's own roughly three-year history. Unusual against the past six months, mid-range against its short full record.
history_html:
The level, said honestly. This run's peak, Monday's 5.31%, was the 10-year's highest since May 2002; Friday's 5.24% sits below it. Against the last 30 years that's high (87th percentile). Since 1962 it's average (49th), and every reading in the 1970s and 1980s was higher.

Is it 2007 again? Against June 2007, the 10-year's last visit before this run, the 10-year, real yields, the term premium (a Fed model's estimate of the extra yield for lending long) and credit all match. Three things differ: the Fed's rate (5.26% then, SOFR 3.87% now), mortgage rates (6.53% then, 7.40% now) and stocks, nearer a record now.

Short records need the long view. TIPS real yields start in 2003; the Cleveland Fed's longer record puts real rates at the 80th percentile of the last 30 years but the 54th since 1982. Junk spreads have only a three-year record here; the long-run investment-grade proxy (Baa minus the 10-year, dated 10-06) sits at the 3rd percentile since 1986 (2nd over 30 years): still tight.

Speed is the rarer part. This year's 106bp rise ties 1980's as the 8th-largest through this date since 1963. From the start of the 14 past 12-month rises this big (1.10 points or more), a recession began within two years in 6 of 13 and stocks were lower a year later in 5 of 14, against about one in four normally. Two of the six were one recession; 13 is a small sample.

Why this matters (client-ready): “Rates are high for anyone who started investing after the mid-'90s, average since 1962, and lower than any day of the '70s or '80s. When rates rose this fast before, a recession followed within two years in 6 of 13 cases, versus about one in four normally: a small sample, not a forecast.”
concept_title: The dollar moves in long waves: read today's level against the whole cycle
concept_html: The first three segments covered how a strong dollar tightens conditions, why carry pulls money toward higher U.S. rates, and how that tightening spreads abroad. Today's piece is about time scale. The dollar doesn't swing day to day the way stocks do; it moves in waves that last years. So two yardsticks answer two different questions. The 120-day z-score (+2.04 on Friday) says the dollar is strong compared with the past six months. The long record says where that sits in the cycle. Since 1971, DXY (the dollar against a basket of major currencies) has ranged from 71.33, its 2000s low, to 164.72, its 1980s high. Friday's 102.21 is the 72nd percentile of that whole history and the 81st of the last 30 years. By decade, the dollar was at or above Friday's level on 57.7% of days in the 1980s, but on only 1.6% of days in the 1990s and 0.6% in the 2010s. Its latest peak, 114.11 in September 2022, was well above today. Put together: strong by recent memory, inside the long range. That matters for clients with international funds, since a dollar this strong shrinks what foreign holdings are worth in dollars, and the long record says it has gone both higher and much lower.
client_translation: The dollar moves in long waves: it's strong right now for anyone who remembers the 2010s, but ordinary for anyone who remembers the '80s, and over years it can swing a long way in either direction.
masthead_title: Junk-bond spreads widened again on Thursday, the selloff day, and stocks bounced back Friday to within 0.1% of their record.
regime_line: Today's defining fact: junk-bond spreads widened to 3.15% on Thursday, the day of the tech selloff (the print filled in this morning), refuting this system's claim that credit would shrug off this week's rate jump; Friday's credit print isn't in yet, and that day the S&P 500 rose 0.59% to within 0.10% of its record close while the 10-year rose 2bp to 5.24%.
story_html:
A wire story carried by The Washington Post and other papers was headlined Friday “Wall Street finishes its record-setting week with gains”: the S&P 500 rose 0.59% to 7,811.54, its first gain since its Oct 6 record. CNBC led with the Dow’s 400-point rise and a winning week. The day’s biggest single-stock story was telecom. CNBC tied a sharp selloff in T-Mobile, Verizon and AT&T to SpaceX’s deal, announced Thursday evening and pending FCC approval, to buy 800 MHz spectrum from Grain Management for its Starlink Mobile service. Separately, Bloomberg reported Friday that OpenAI expects at least $70 billion in annualized revenue by the end of 2026; the same report put the figure at about $50 billion at the end of September. Reuters had oil settling slightly higher, with Gulf of Mexico producers shutting in about 63% of output as of Thursday ahead of a hurricane, and gains pared after President Trump pledged no attack on Iran before the Nov. 3 midterms.

Does this system’s own data confirm that framing? On stocks, yes, and broadly: the equal-weight S&P proxy (RSP, the average stock) rose 0.55%, about in line with SPY’s +0.60%, and the S&P 500 ended the week up 1.15%. On tech, only partly. The Nasdaq rose 0.64%, but the chip fund SMH fell 0.65%, its fifth straight session behind SPY, and it lost 4.32% on the week. No major outlet gave a reason for the chip lag that this system could find, so none is claimed. On rates, the 10-year rose 2bp to 5.24%. It first reached that level on Sep 28 and has been there on 9 of the 10 sessions since; before this run, it last got there only briefly, in June 2007 (Today in history, below). Oil: WTI rose 0.39% to $91.85, matching Reuters’ settle; the reasons are Reuters’, untested here.

The new piece is credit. This morning’s pull filled in Thursday’s high-yield spread (HY OAS, §5): it widened 6bp to 3.15%, after 3.09% the day before. That refutes CL-0036 (Claims, above) and gives a clear answer to what the 10-09 edition said would be the real test: on the selloff day, junk-bond spreads widened while investment-grade spreads held flat. A new claim, CL-0041, tests whether that widening holds. Friday’s own credit print arrives on a later run.

Friday’s one scheduled release missed: the University of Michigan’s preliminary October consumer sentiment index came in at 46.3 (Bloomberg; the median forecast in Bloomberg’s survey was 47.6), down from 48.1 in September. Year-ahead inflation expectations rose to 4.7% from 4.6%. Bloomberg reported that views of current conditions hit an all-time low; this system holds no sentiment history to check that (§4F), so it stays Bloomberg’s framing.
movers_html:
How this section works: all 504 S&P constituents scanned mechanically (503 of 504 covered); a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest), never by seeming interesting. 31 name candidates and 1 sector divergence qualified; cap is 3 names + 1 sector note. Moderna (+14.21%, the scan’s second-largest gain) is left out: The Motley Fool tied the jump to reports of a major new cancer-research initiative, with no macro read-through. (Moderna also joined the Nasdaq-100 before Friday’s open, per Nasdaq; no outlet seen tied the move to that.) Note on the basis: the scan measures each move from the prior close; Verizon and AT&T both went ex-dividend Friday, so their raw moves below include the dividend.

T-Mobile (TMUS) −13.27% (148.58, from 171.31) — what happened: the scan’s largest decline, alongside AT&T (−10.82% raw, −9.81% after its $0.278 dividend went ex Friday) and Verizon (−10.14% raw, −8.75% after its $0.708 dividend). Stated reason: CNBC tied the carrier selloff to SpaceX’s deal, announced Thursday evening and pending FCC approval, to buy up to 14 MHz of paired 800 MHz spectrum from Grain Management for Starlink Mobile. CNBC quoted a JPMorgan note seeing the long-term opportunity as “more credible” but “limited near-term risk to U.S. wireless incumbents given the time, infrastructure and capital required to build a competitive terrestrial network.” Read-through: a competition shock to an industry with three national carriers, not a macro signal. It matters for income portfolios, since the three carriers are widely held for their dividends. New claim CL-0040 tests whether the repricing holds.

Crown Castle (CCI) +15.61% (79.64, from 68.89) — what happened: the scan’s largest gain, with American Tower +9.30% and SBA Communications +7.34%. Stated reason: the same SpaceX deal, read the other way. CNBC reported the tower companies rising on the prospect of SpaceX as a new tenant, and ran a Bernstein analyst (Madison Rezaei) saying the plan is good for tower operators. Read-through: sector-specific. CNBC’s reporting is about a possible new tenant, which would mean more tower rent if a lease is ever signed. No macro read-through.

Humana (HUM) +11.56% (431.87, from 387.12) — what happened: a large gain in managed care. Stated reason: Humana said 95% of its Medicare Advantage members will be in plans rated 4 stars or higher for 2027, after the government’s star ratings came out Thursday (company statement, carried by Investing.com and StockTitan). Star ratings set the quality-bonus payments these plans can earn. Read-through: idiosyncratic and regulatory: a scoring outcome for one company, no macro read-through.

Sector note — Communication Services (XLC) −1.51% vs. SPY +0.60%. The only sector fund to trail the market by 1.5 points or more, on the day its carrier members fell sharply (above). Nothing in today’s search reported a second driver, so none is claimed.
tier3_html: Daily read: SMH (this system’s chip-fund proxy for AI capex) fell 0.65% Friday against SPY’s +0.60%, a fifth straight session behind, and lost 4.32% on the week. Bloomberg reported Friday that OpenAI expects at least $70 billion in annualized revenue by the end of 2026; the same report put the figure at about $50 billion at the end of September. Oracle, whose Thursday drop CL-0039 is testing, rebounded 4.21% to $141.40, now $1.07 short of that claim’s $142.47 refute line (+5%). The optics names steadied too: Bloomberg TV ran Lumentum’s CEO saying its optical-parts capacity is sold out to 2029, and Lumentum (+5.22%), Ciena (+5.60%) and Coherent (+3.40%) all rose. But chips as a group didn’t follow. On financing, Reuters reported that Nvidia-backed Firmus scrapped its roughly $5 billion Australian IPO, citing market volatility, and will raise money privately instead: one data point of a large AI-infrastructure listing stepping back from public markets this week. Why this matters: the AI-capex story now has a demand-side number (OpenAI’s) and a supply-side one (Lumentum’s) pointing up, while the chip index that tracks it has lagged five sessions running. Claims CL-0038 and CL-0039 grade which one the market believes by Oct 16.
calendar_note_html: No releases on a Saturday. Friday’s results: University of Michigan preliminary sentiment 46.3 against Bloomberg’s 47.6 median forecast, with year-ahead inflation expectations up to 4.7% from 4.6% (Story, above). A Boston Fed (Collins) appearance was on the calendar for 4pm ET Friday; no coverage of what was said turned up, so nothing is reported. Next week’s calendar loads with Monday’s refresh; Monday is the Columbus Day holiday. Why this matters to the current regime: households expecting a little more inflation while the 10-year sits at 5.24% is the backdrop for the Fed’s next decision. Next week’s 10-year breakeven prints (the bond market’s own inflation forecast) are this system’s check on whether the bond market agrees (Unit 2).
client_lens_html:
“What happened to my phone-company stocks?” Reporting (CNBC) ties Friday’s drop in T-Mobile, Verizon and AT&T to SpaceX buying wireless spectrum for a possible fourth national network. Two details worth having ready. First, Verizon and AT&T both went ex-dividend Friday, so part of their price drop is the dividend itself, which holders still receive. Second, JPMorgan’s note (via CNBC) saw limited near-term risk because building a competing network takes time, infrastructure and a lot of capital. CL-0040 tracks whether the drop holds.

“Is the market at a record again?” Almost: the S&P 500 closed 0.10% below its Oct 6 record, up 1.15% on the week, and the average stock kept pace. The caveat is under the surface. Junk-bond spreads widened two prints in a row, and chips have lagged five sessions running. So it’s a strong week for the index, with the riskiest corner of the bond market a little more cautious.

“Are interest rates still going up?” The 10-year ended the week at 5.24%, down from Monday’s 5.31% peak. That’s high against the last 30 years (87th percentile) but average since 1962 (49th), and every reading in the 1970s and 1980s was higher (Today in history, above). Consumers expect a little more inflation this month (year-ahead expectations at 4.7%, per the University of Michigan survey), a reading the Fed watches closely.

  • Rules test (the §4F history rules on a fresh day): (1) Continuity: the 10-year dipped to 5.22% Thursday, so the History check says “first reached this level on Sep 28 and has been there on 9 of the 10 sessions since” instead of “since Sep 28.” (2) Cutoff-dependent pairs: high real yields with tight credit is still in its extreme band, but its past-case count depends on the cutoff, so it stays out of the History check and no track record is claimed. (3) Short records: TIPS reads “extreme since 2003 (short record)” with the Cleveland Fed’s longer record beside it (high against the last 30 years, about average since 1982), and the dashboard shows one number, not a fake 30-year view. (4) Then vs. now: the panel’s anchor moved from June 14 to June 12, 2007, because Friday’s 5.24% sets a slightly higher bar than Thursday’s 5.22%. That two-day shift alone changed three calls: the S&P 500 was 3.0% below its record on June 12, 2007 but 1.1% below on June 14, the mortgage rate comes from a different week, and the 2s10s curve (+18bp on June 12 vs. +13bp on June 14) flips from different to similar. A single-day anchor is fragile; logged to the backlog. (5) Lagged prints: Thursday’s credit print is used to grade Thursday’s selloff, not Friday’s rebound. (6) Prose checks: the history interpretation’s first drafts ran over the 300-word cap and were cut, and the cut briefly dropped the Cleveland cross-check that the rules require whenever real yields are cited (restored). An independent check of the finished draft then found mistakes the linter had let through: junk-bond spreads called “far outside” their six-month range when Oct 1’s 3.24% was higher, a hurricane name and a sentiment figure no recorded source showed, an Associated Press label the search results never confirmed, and a regime line that set Thursday’s credit print against Friday’s stocks. All are fixed above. The linter was then tightened against the gaps it exposed: it now reads “junk-bond spreads” as HY OAS, rejects “outside its six-month range” when the data says otherwise, rejects “N-month high” superlatives for the two short-record spreads, checks “has been above X since” against every reading, checks decade claims against the by-decade data, and blocks a lagged print tied to the wrong weekday. The final copy passes it.
